::: {.lm-hero}
[Chapter 10 · Representation Learning]{.eyebrow}

# Convolutional Networks

[*One filter, slid across every position: weight sharing is a structured prior, and it is what lets a network learn to see.*]{.dek}
:::

A dense network treats every pixel as unrelated to its neighbors. For an image that is both a poor assumption and an extravagant number of parameters: a fully connected layer over a 28&times;28 digit needs a separate weight for every pixel-to-unit pair. A [convolutional network]{.term} assumes something instead. The same small [filter]{.term} (a kernel of a few weights) is applied at every location, so a pattern learned in one corner is recognized everywhere. The book reads this weight sharing as an [infinitely strong prior]{.term}, the spatial cousin of the regularization in Chapter 7: rather than learn that nearby pixels are related, the architecture bakes it in.

The operation itself is concrete. A 2D convolution slides the filter across the image and computes a dot product at each position. The result is a [feature map]{.term} that lights up wherever the filter's pattern appears.

::: {.defbox}
[2D Convolution]{.lbl}

[ (X &lowast; W)<sub>i, j</sub> = &Sigma;<sub>p, q</sub> &thinsp; X<sub>i+p, j+q</sub> &middot; W<sub>p, q</sub> ]{.math}
:::

Strictly, that is *cross-correlation*: true convolution flips the filter, summing $X_{i-p,\,j-q} W_{p,q}$. Deep-learning frameworks implement cross-correlation and call it convolution, and since the filter weights are learned rather than designed, the distinction makes no difference to anything below. We follow the convention, as the book does.

```{=html}
<figure class="lm-figure">
<img src="../figures/ch10_01_convnets.png?v=8a25f63f" alt="Three panels joined by an asterisk and an equals sign, so the row reads as the convolution equation. Left: a 10 by 10 input image, a gray square of ones on a pale field of zeros, with a red 3 by 3 outline marking the filter window at row 2, column 1; the nine values under that window are printed in their cells, a column of zeros and two columns of ones. Center: the 3 by 3 vertical-edge kernel as a heatmap with cell borders, a blue column of minus ones, a pale column of zeros, and a red column of plus ones, each cell labeled with its weight. Right: the resulting 8 by 8 feature map, deep red in the two columns straddling the square's left edge, deep blue in the two columns straddling its right edge, and flat pale in between, with a red circle and the label plus 3 marking the output pixel produced by the highlighted window.">
<figcaption><strong>One filter, one pass.</strong> Read the row as the equation above it. The window outlined in red sits over nine input values, printed in place: a column of zeros and two columns of ones. Multiply them by the kernel and sum &mdash; the minus ones fall on zeros and the zero column adds nothing, so only the right-hand column of plus ones counts, three times over &mdash; and the result is the +3 circled in the feature map. Sliding the window over every valid position produces the whole map: strong positive response along the square's left edge, equally strong negative along its right, and nothing at all where the image is flat. The input is gray rather than blue so that blue can mean one thing throughout, negative. This is the result the code below reproduces.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

## One filter, four placements

First, the chapter's own example (Section 10.2): a 3&times;3 input and a 2&times;2 filter, four placements, and the feature map the book prints, $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 0],
              [0, 1, 3],
              [2, 1, 0]])
W = np.array([[1,  0],
              [0, -1]])

out = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
for i in range(2):
    for j in range(2):
        out[i, j] = np.sum(X[i:i+2, j:j+2] * W)   # one placement of the filter
print(out)                                         # the book: [[0, -1], [-1, 1]]
```

## R
```{webr}
X <- matrix(c(1, 2, 0,
              0, 1, 3,
              2, 1, 0), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
W <- matrix(c(1,  0,
              0, -1), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

out <- matrix(0, 2, 2)
for (i in 1:2) for (j in 1:2)
  out[i, j] <- sum(X[i:(i + 1), j:(j + 1)] * W)   # one placement of the filter
print(out)                                        # the book: [[0, -1], [-1, 1]]
```

:::

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  const root = document.getElementById('ix-conv'), L = window.LMIX, $ = s => root.querySelector(s);
  // Two inputs: the book's 3x3 example with its 2x2 filter, and the by-hand cell's square with its vertical-edge filter.
  const BOOK = { name: 'book', X: [[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 3], [2, 1, 0]], W: [[1, 0], [0, -1]], ms: 650 };
  const SQ = (function () {
    const X = []; for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) { X.push([]); for (let j = 0; j < 10; j++) X[i].push(i >= 2 && i < 8 && j >= 2 && j < 8 ? 1 : 0); }
    return { name: 'square', X: X, W: [[-1, 0, 1], [-1, 0, 1], [-1, 0, 1]], ms: 160 };
  })();
  let ex = BOOK, k = 0, timer = null;                    // k = placements done so far
  const n = () => ex.X.length, kk = () => ex.W.length, o = () => n() - kk() + 1, N = () => o() * o();
  const pos = t => [Math.floor(t / o()), t % o()];        // placement t -> (row, col) of the output
  const sumAt = (i, j) => { let s = 0; for (let p = 0; p < kk(); p++) for (let q = 0; q < kk(); q++) s += ex.X[i + p][j + q] * ex.W[p][q]; return s; };
  const neg = v => v < 0 ? '(' + v + ')' : String(v);

  function grid(svg, M, x0, y0, cell, C, text) {
    for (let i = 0; i < M.length; i++) for (let j = 0; j < M[0].length; j++) {
      L.el('rect', { x: x0 + j * cell, y: y0 + i * cell, width: cell, height: cell, fill: text(i, j).fill, stroke: C.axis }, svg);
      const t = text(i, j).label;
      if (t !== null) L.el('text', { x: x0 + (j + 0.5) * cell, y: y0 + (i + 0.5) * cell + cell * 0.14, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': text(i, j).size, fill: text(i, j).ink }, svg).textContent = t;
    }
  }
  function drawIn(C) {
    const svg = $('.ix-in'); svg.innerHTML = '';
    const cell = Math.min(360 / n(), 90), x0 = (400 - cell * n()) / 2, y0 = 6;
    const cur = k < N() ? pos(k) : pos(N() - 1);
    grid(svg, ex.X, x0, y0, cell, C, (i, j) => ({ fill: ex.X[i][j] ? (ex.name === 'square' ? '#d9d6cc' : '#fff') : '#fff', label: String(ex.X[i][j]), size: n() > 5 ? 13 : 26, ink: C.ink }));
    L.el('rect', { x: x0 + cur[1] * cell, y: y0 + cur[0] * cell, width: cell * kk(), height: cell * kk(), fill: 'none', stroke: C.red, 'stroke-width': 3 }, svg);
    const kc = Math.min(44, cell), kx = (400 - kc * kk()) / 2, ky = y0 + cell * n() + 34;
    L.el('text', { x: 200, y: ky - 10, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 14, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = 'the filter';
    grid(svg, ex.W, kx, ky, kc, C, (i, j) => ({ fill: ex.W[i][j] > 0 ? 'rgba(7,111,161,0.16)' : ex.W[i][j] < 0 ? 'rgba(227,18,11,0.12)' : '#fff', label: String(ex.W[i][j]), size: 18, ink: C.ink }));
  }
  function drawOut(C) {
    const svg = $('.ix-out'); svg.innerHTML = '';
    const cell = Math.min(360 / o(), 90), x0 = (400 - cell * o()) / 2, y0 = (400 - cell * o()) / 2;
    const cur = k > 0 ? pos(k - 1) : null;
    grid(svg, Array.from({ length: o() }, (_, i) => Array.from({ length: o() }, (_, j) => i * o() + j)), x0, y0, cell, C, (i, j) => {
      const t = i * o() + j, done = t < k, v = done ? sumAt(i, j) : 0;
      return { fill: !done ? '#fff' : cur && cur[0] === i && cur[1] === j ? 'rgba(7,111,161,0.28)' : v > 0 ? 'rgba(7,111,161,0.12)' : v < 0 ? 'rgba(227,18,11,0.10)' : '#f6f5f0',
               label: done ? String(v) : null, size: o() > 4 ? 15 : 26, ink: C.ink };
    });
  }
  function equation(C) {
    const box = $('.m-eq'); box.innerHTML = '';
    if (k === 0) { box.innerHTML = '<span class="lhs">Press Step to place the filter.</span>'; return; }
    const p = pos(k - 1); let terms = [];
    for (let a = 0; a < kk(); a++) for (let b = 0; b < kk(); b++) terms.push(neg(ex.X[p[0] + a][p[1] + b]) + '·' + neg(ex.W[a][b]));
    const s = sumAt(p[0], p[1]);
    const txt = (ex.name === 'square' && terms.length === 9) ? terms.slice(0, 3).join(' + ') + ' + … + ' + terms.slice(6).join(' + ') : terms.join(' + ');
    box.innerHTML = '<span class="lhs">row ' + (p[0] + 1) + ', column ' + (p[1] + 1) + ':</span><span>' + txt + ' = <b>' + s + '</b></span>';
  }
  function note() {
    if (ex.name === 'book') {
      const book = ['Placing the filter at the top left and summing the elementwise products gives (1)(1) + (2)(0) + (0)(0) + (1)(−1) = 0.',
                    'One step to the right: (2)(1) + (0)(0) + (1)(0) + (3)(−1) = −1.',
                    'Down one row, back to the left: (0)(1) + (1)(0) + (2)(0) + (1)(−1) = −1.',
                    'The last placement gives (1)(1) + (3)(0) + (1)(0) + (0)(−1) = 1, and the map is complete: a 3×3 input and a 2×2 filter leave (3 − 2)/1 + 1 = 2 positions along each side, so the map is 2×2. The same four sums, in the same order, are what the cell above computes.'];
      return k === 0 ? 'The book\'s example: a 3×3 input, a 2×2 filter, four placements. Step through them.' : book[k - 1];
    }
    if (k === 0) return 'The square of ones from the cell below, with the vertical-edge filter: right column minus left. Play it and watch where the response is positive, where it is negative, and where it is zero.';
    const p = pos(k - 1), s = sumAt(p[0], p[1]);
    if (s > 0) return 'The window straddles the square\'s left edge: its right column sits on ones and its left on zeros, so the response is +' + s + '. The filter fires where the image goes from dark to light, left to right.';
    if (s < 0) return 'The window straddles the right edge: ones on the left, zeros on the right, so the response is ' + s + '. Same edge, opposite sign.';
    return 'Both columns of the window carry the same total, so the response is exactly zero. That is every flat place in the image, inside the square as well as outside it: the filter sees change, and nothing else.';
  }
  function update() {
    const C = L.colors(root);
    drawIn(C); drawOut(C); equation(C);
    L.stat($('.t-k'), 0, k === N(), () => k + ' of ' + N());
    L.stat($('.t-n'), 0, false, () => '(' + n() + ' − ' + kk() + ')/1 + 1 = ' + o() + ', so ' + o() + '×' + o());
    $('.ix-note').textContent = note();
  }
  function stop() { clearInterval(timer); timer = null; }
  function step() { if (k < N()) { k++; update(); } if (k >= N()) stop(); }
  function play() { stop(); if (k >= N()) k = 0; timer = setInterval(step, ex.ms); step(); }
  function setEx(e) { stop(); ex = e; k = 0; $('.p-book').classList.toggle('on', e === BOOK); $('.p-sq').classList.toggle('on', e === SQ); update(); }
  const bar = $('.ix-buttons');
  L.presets(bar, [
    { label: 'Step', action: () => { stop(); step(); } },
    { label: 'Play', action: play },
    { label: 'Reset', action: () => setEx(ex) },
  ]);
  const gap = document.createElement('div'); gap.className = 'gap'; bar.appendChild(gap);
  L.presets(bar, [
    { label: 'The book\'s 3×3 example', action: () => setEx(BOOK) },
    { label: 'The square and the edge filter', action: () => setEx(SQ) },
  ]);
  bar.children[4].classList.add('p-book'); bar.children[5].classList.add('p-sq');
  setEx(BOOK);
})();
</script>
</div>
```

## The convolution, by hand

The operation needs no deep-learning framework, so this part runs here in the browser. We build a square of ones on a field of zeros, design a vertical-edge kernel, slide it by hand, and read the feature map. The cell is pure NumPy on the Python side and base R on the other.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle

def conv2d(image, kernel):
    """2D convolution, no padding, stride 1."""
    H, W = image.shape
    kH, kW = kernel.shape
    out = np.zeros((H - kH + 1, W - kW + 1))
    for i in range(out.shape[0]):
        for j in range(out.shape[1]):
            patch = image[i:i+kH, j:j+kW]          # the window under the filter
            out[i, j] = np.sum(patch * kernel)     # dot product at this position
    return out

image = np.zeros((10, 10))
image[2:8, 2:8] = 1.0                              # a square of ones on a field of zeros

kernel = np.array([[-1., 0., 1.],
                   [-1., 0., 1.],
                   [-1., 0., 1.]])                 # +ve on dark -> light, left to right

feature_map = conv2d(image, kernel)

si, sj = 2, 1                                      # one window, written out in full
patch = image[si:si+3, sj:sj+3]
print(f"input {image.shape} * kernel {kernel.shape} -> feature map {feature_map.shape}")
print(f"patch under the window:\n{patch.astype(int)}")
print(f"patch . kernel = {np.sum(patch * kernel):+.0f}  (= feature_map[{si}, {sj}])")
print(f"response runs {feature_map.min():+.0f} to {feature_map.max():+.0f}; "
      f"{int((feature_map == 0).sum())} of {feature_map.size} entries are exactly 0")
print(f"left edge, top to bottom: {feature_map[:, 0].astype(int)}")

SPINE, RED = "#cfccc2", "#E3120B"
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11.2, 4.3))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 3, wspace=0.36)
axI, axK, axF = (fig.add_subplot(gs[0, k]) for k in range(3))

# Gray, not blue: blue means "negative" in the other two panels, and one ink
# cannot also mean "pixel is on". vmin/vmax are stretched past the data so a 1
# lands on mid-gray rather than black.
axI.imshow(image, cmap="Greys", vmin=-0.13, vmax=1.48, interpolation="nearest")
axI.add_patch(Rectangle((sj - 0.5, si - 0.5), 3, 3, fill=False, edgecolor=RED,
                        lw=2.0, label=f"filter window at row {si}, col {sj}", zorder=4))
for i in range(si, si + 3):                        # the nine numbers being multiplied
    for j in range(sj, sj + 3):
        axI.text(j, i, f"{image[i, j]:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9,
                 color="white" if image[i, j] > 0.5 else "#333333", zorder=5)
axI.set_title("input image  (10 × 10)", fontsize=11)
axI.set_xticks(range(0, 10, 2)); axI.set_yticks(range(0, 10, 2))
axI.legend(loc="lower center", frameon=True, facecolor="white", framealpha=0.92,
           edgecolor=SPINE, fontsize=8.5, handlelength=1.2)

axK.imshow(kernel, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1.6, vmax=1.6, interpolation="nearest")
axK.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, 3, 1), minor=True)  # cell borders: a 3x3, not 3 bars
axK.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, 3, 1), minor=True)
axK.grid(which="minor", color=SPINE, lw=1.4); axK.tick_params(which="minor", length=0)
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        label = f"{kernel[i, j]:+.0f}" if kernel[i, j] else "0"   # zero has no sign
        axK.text(j, i, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13, color="#333333")
axK.set_title("vertical-edge kernel  (3 × 3)", fontsize=11)
axK.set_xlabel("weights −1, 0, +1", fontsize=9, color="#666666", labelpad=6)
axK.set_xticks([]); axK.set_yticks([])

im = axF.imshow(feature_map, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-3, vmax=3, interpolation="nearest")
axF.scatter([sj], [si], s=70, facecolors="none", edgecolors=RED, linewidths=2.0)
axF.annotate(f"{feature_map[si, sj]:+.0f}", xy=(sj + 0.55, si), fontsize=11,
             fontweight="bold", color=RED, ha="left", va="center")
axF.set_title("feature map  (8 × 8)", fontsize=11)
axF.set_xticks(range(0, 8, 2)); axF.set_yticks(range(0, 8, 2))

for ax in (axI, axK, axF):
    for s in ax.spines.values():
        s.set_color(SPINE)
    ax.tick_params(colors="#666666", labelsize=9, length=3)

# Panel boxes are only final once aspect='equal' is applied, so draw first. The
# colorbar then gets its own axes at the feature map's exact height rather than
# being carved out of it, which would leave the result the smallest of the three.
fig.canvas.draw()
pI, pK, pF = (ax.get_position() for ax in (axI, axK, axF))
cb = fig.colorbar(im, cax=fig.add_axes([pF.x1 + 0.014, pF.y0, 0.014, pF.height]))
cb.set_label("response", fontsize=10); cb.set_ticks([-3, 0, 3])
cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=9, colors="#666666"); cb.outline.set_edgecolor(SPINE)

y_mid = (pI.y0 + pI.y1) / 2                        # read the row as an equation
fig.text((pI.x1 + pK.x0) / 2, y_mid, "∗", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=19, color="#666666")
fig.text((pK.x1 + pF.x0) / 2, y_mid, "=", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=19, color="#666666")

plt.show()
```

## R
```{webr}
conv2d <- function(img, ker) {          # 2D convolution, no padding, stride 1
  kH <- nrow(ker); kW <- ncol(ker)
  out <- matrix(0, nrow(img) - kH + 1, ncol(img) - kW + 1)
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(out))) {
    for (j in seq_len(ncol(out))) {
      patch <- img[i:(i + kH - 1), j:(j + kW - 1)]   # the window under the filter
      out[i, j] <- sum(patch * ker)                  # dot product at this position
    }
  }
  out
}

img <- matrix(0, 10, 10)
img[3:8, 3:8] <- 1                      # a square of ones on a field of zeros (1-based)

ker <- matrix(c(-1, 0, 1,
                -1, 0, 1,
                -1, 0, 1), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)   # +ve on dark -> light

feature_map <- conv2d(img, ker)

si <- 2; sj <- 1                        # one window, written out in full (0-based)
patch <- img[(si + 1):(si + 3), (sj + 1):(sj + 3)]
cat(sprintf("input (%d, %d) * kernel (%d, %d) -> feature map (%d, %d)\n",
            nrow(img), ncol(img), nrow(ker), ncol(ker),
            nrow(feature_map), ncol(feature_map)))
cat("patch under the window:\n"); print(patch)
cat(sprintf("patch . kernel = %+d  (= feature_map[%d, %d])\n",
            as.integer(sum(patch * ker)), si, sj))
cat(sprintf("response runs %+d to %+d; %d of %d entries are exactly 0\n",
            as.integer(min(feature_map)), as.integer(max(feature_map)),
            sum(feature_map == 0), length(feature_map)))
cat("left edge, top to bottom:", feature_map[, 1], "\n")

SPINE <- "#cfccc2"; RED <- "#E3120B"
# Gray for the input: blue means "negative" in the other two panels, and one ink
# cannot also mean "pixel is on". The ramp stops short of black on purpose.
greys <- colorRampPalette(c("#f2f2f2", "#4d4d4d"))(64)
divg  <- colorRampPalette(c("#08306b", "#4292c6", "#f7f7f7", "#d6604d", "#67000d"))(64)

# image() wants z[x, y] with y running upward, so transpose and flip the rows
as_picture <- function(m) t(m)[, nrow(m):1]

panel <- function(m, col, zlim, main, ticks) {
  image(x = 0:(ncol(m) - 1), y = 0:(nrow(m) - 1), z = as_picture(m),
        col = col, zlim = zlim, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
        main = main, asp = 1)
  if (!is.null(ticks)) {
    axis(1, at = ticks, labels = ticks, col = SPINE, col.axis = "#666666", cex.axis = 0.8)
    axis(2, at = nrow(m) - 1 - ticks, labels = ticks, col = SPINE,
         col.axis = "#666666", cex.axis = 0.8, las = 1)
  }
  box(col = SPINE)
}

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3, 2.5, 3, 2.5))

panel(img, greys, c(0, 1), "input image  (10 x 10)", seq(0, 8, by = 2))
rect(sj - 0.5, nrow(img) - 1 - (si + 2) - 0.5, sj + 2.5, nrow(img) - 1 - si + 0.5,
     border = RED, lwd = 2)
for (i in (si + 1):(si + 3)) for (j in (sj + 1):(sj + 3))   # the nine numbers multiplied
  text(j - 1, nrow(img) - i, img[i, j], cex = 0.75,
       col = if (img[i, j] > 0.5) "white" else "#333333")
legend("bottom", sprintf("filter window at row %d, col %d", si, sj),
       pch = 0, col = RED, pt.lwd = 2, bg = "white", box.col = SPINE, cex = 0.75)
mtext("*", side = 4, line = 0.6, las = 1, cex = 1.6, col = "#666666")

panel(ker, divg, c(-1.6, 1.6), "vertical-edge kernel  (3 x 3)", NULL)
abline(h = c(0.5, 1.5), v = c(0.5, 1.5), col = SPINE, lwd = 1.4)  # a 3x3, not 3 bars
for (i in 1:3) for (j in 1:3)
  text(j - 1, 3 - i, if (ker[i, j] == 0) "0" else sprintf("%+d", ker[i, j]), cex = 1.1)
mtext("weights -1, 0, +1", side = 1, line = 1.1, cex = 0.7, col = "#666666")
mtext("=", side = 4, line = 0.6, las = 1, cex = 1.6, col = "#666666")

panel(feature_map, divg, c(-3, 3), "feature map  (8 x 8)", seq(0, 6, by = 2))
points(sj, nrow(feature_map) - 1 - si, pch = 1, col = RED, cex = 2, lwd = 2)
text(sj + 0.6, nrow(feature_map) - 1 - si,          # inline, so the zero band stays clear
     sprintf("%+d", as.integer(feature_map[si + 1, sj + 1])),
     col = RED, font = 2, adj = 0, cex = 0.95)

par(op)
```

:::

Four things in that output are worth pausing on. The map is 8&times;8, two pixels narrower and shorter than the 10&times;10 input, because a 3&times;3 window has only eight valid positions along a side; this is what `padding` exists to undo. Half of it &mdash; 32 of 64 entries &mdash; is exactly zero, and the zeros are precisely the flat places: the response is the window's right column minus its left, so it vanishes wherever those two carry the same total. The nonzero response is confined to the two column bands that straddle the square's vertical edges: positive on the left, where the image goes dark to light, negative on the right, where it goes light to dark. And the largest magnitude is 3, the sum of the kernel's positive weights, reached only where all three rows of the window sit on the edge &mdash; the printed left-edge column, `1 2 3 3 3 3 2 1`, shows the response weakening at the top and bottom, where the window overhangs the square and only one or two of its rows overlap.

Swapping the kernel for `[[-1,-1,-1],[0,0,0],[1,1,1]]` rotates the whole story a quarter turn: the response is positive along the square's top edge, peaking at +3, and negative along its bottom. Each filter sees one kind of structure and is blind to the rest, which is why a layer holds a bank of them rather than one. The point of the chapter is that we will not design these by hand for long. A trained network learns its own filters, and visualizations of trained networks suggest that early layers respond to edges at different orientations and simple contrasts (Zeiler and Fergus 2014, the study the book cites). Whether a particular small network's first layer ends up looking like these detectors is an empirical question; the [applied page](ch10_02_applied.qmd) measures one whose 3&times;3 filters barely leave their random initialization.

## Stacking it into a network

[Pooling]{.term} follows convolution to shrink the feature maps. Max pooling keeps the strongest activation in each small window, which reduces computation and can make the representation less sensitive to small shifts: the maximum is unchanged when a response moves within its window. Convolution gives equivariance (shift the input, shift the feature map). Pooling does not guarantee [translation invariance]{.term}, though, since a shift that moves a response across a window boundary can change the pooled output.

A working architecture stacks these into blocks. Each block is convolution, then a ReLU nonlinearity, then pooling; a few blocks build a hierarchy where early layers detect edges and strokes and later layers assemble them into shapes. The stack ends by flattening the final feature maps and passing them to a fully connected head, which is the same affine-plus-softmax classifier from Chapter 4, now a generalized linear model on *learned* features instead of raw pixels.

The rest of this page runs in **Google Colab**, not in the browser: the model is built and trained in PyTorch with `torchvision` for the MNIST data, which is far too heavy for a browser sandbox, and a GPU turns minutes of training into seconds. The code below is for reference; open it in Colab to run and change it.

```{=html}
<a class="colab-btn" href="https://colab.research.google.com/github/welr/learning_machines/blob/main/ch10_01_convnets.ipynb" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><span class="dot"></span> Open in Google Colab</a>
```

`nn.Conv2d` is the loop above, with batches, multiple channels, and the GPU handled for you. Two parameters shape the output: `stride` (how far the filter moves each step) and `padding` (zeros around the border; `padding=1` with a 3&times;3 filter keeps the output the same size as the input). The network below stacks two convolutional blocks and a linear head.

```python
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class SimpleCNN(nn.Module):
    """Conv -> ReLU -> Pool, twice, then a GLM head."""
    def __init__(self, n_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1)   # one filter bank, slid everywhere
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.pool  = nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2)
        self.fc1   = nn.Linear(32 * 7 * 7, 64)                    # 28 -> 14 -> 7 after two poolings
        self.fc2   = nn.Linear(64, n_classes)                    # affine + softmax: the Chapter 4 classifier

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv1(x)))                     # 28x28 -> 14x14
        x = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv2(x)))                     # 14x14 -> 7x7
        x = x.flatten(1)                                         # hand the learned features to the head
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        return self.fc2(x)
```

Training is the loop from Chapter 3, unchanged in principle. We load MNIST, then for each batch run a forward pass, compute the cross-entropy loss, let `loss.backward()` supply the gradients by backpropagation, and step the optimizer.

```python
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from torchvision import datasets, transforms

device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize((0.1307,), (0.3081,)),   # MNIST mean and std
])
train_loader = DataLoader(datasets.MNIST('./data', train=True,  download=True, transform=transform),
                          batch_size=64, shuffle=True)

model     = SimpleCNN().to(device)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for epoch in range(5):
    model.train()
    for data, target in train_loader:
        data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(data), target)     # forward pass + loss
        loss.backward()                           # gradients by backprop
        optimizer.step()                          # optimizer update (Adam, Ch 3)
```

Five epochs of this put the notebook's run at 98.4% on the held-out test digits, having peaked at 98.7% after three. Watch the two curves rather than the final number: training accuracy climbs to 99.2% while test accuracy stops improving and drifts down, which is Chapter 6's overfitting picture appearing in a network that most people would call small. The remedy is Chapter 7's, and the notebook's `nn.Dropout` exercise is where to try it. Two other things are worth looking at once it has trained. The first-layer filters, visualized as 3&times;3 images, are worth inspecting rather than assuming: compare them with the edge detectors built by hand at the top of this page. At this size and training budget most of them move little from their random start, so a pattern you can name is the exception. And the feature maps at each layer show the hierarchy at work: the first block responds to edges and strokes, the second, smaller after pooling, responds to higher-level pieces of the digit. The mistakes the model does make tend to fall on ambiguous or poorly written digits, cases where a person might hesitate too.

That is the chapter's claim, made operational. The network is not handed a feature extractor; it learns what to look for, and weight sharing is the prior that makes learning it possible from modest data.

The ratio is the prior expressed in arithmetic. In Colab, add an `nn.Dropout` after `fc1` or swap MNIST for Fashion-MNIST (same shape, harder classes) and watch how the learned filters change.
